subChunks.title: Multi-column Indexes and Index-only Scans
subChunks.hookHtml: A single-column index is the foundation. Composite indexes are the refinement — designed to exactly match the queries your application runs most often.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Composite index

CREATE INDEX idx_comp ON apprentices (rank, xp);

This is useful for queries that filter on rank first, then optionally on xp:

WHERE rank = 'Mage'                  -- uses index
WHERE rank = 'Mage' AND xp > 2000   -- uses index, very efficient
WHERE xp > 2000                     -- does NOT use this index (leading column missing)

The left-prefix rule: a composite index on (A, B, C) supports queries on A, on (A, B), on (A, B, C) — but not on B alone or C alone.

Covering index

-- Query:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';

-- Covering index (includes all queried columns):
CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON apprentices (rank) INCLUDE (name, xp);
-- PostgreSQL INCLUDE syntax. In SQLite/MySQL, list all columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON apprentices (rank, name, xp);

A covering index satisfies the entire query from the index alone — the engine never reads the main table. These produce index-only scans, which are extremely fast.

Index design process

  1. Identify your most frequent/expensive queries
  2. Look at their WHERE and JOIN conditions — index those columns
  3. Add ORDER BY columns to the index when relevant
  4. Add frequently selected columns to INCLUDE (PostgreSQL) for covering indexes

storyBeats.text: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a million-row table — even with an index. Cipher examines the query's WHERE clause.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Composite indexes must lead with the most selective column you filter on first. The left-prefix rule is inflexible — if your WHERE uses only the second column, the composite index is useless. A covering index that holds every column the query needs is the fastest path — the engine never touches the main table.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Index design for a query

Design the optimal index for this query, considering column selectivity. Explain whether a composite or covering index is better:

SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage' AND xp > 3000
ORDER BY xp DESC;
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Optimal index: CREATE INDEX ON apprentices (rank, xp DESC) INCLUDE (name);

Reasoning:
- rank = 'Mage' is an equality filter — it narrows rows the most, so rank is the leading column
- xp > 3000 is a range filter on the second column — with rank first, the index can do an efficient range scan on xp
- ORDER BY xp DESC — storing xp DESC in the index eliminates a separate sort step
- INCLUDE (name) — makes the index covering. The SELECT only needs name and xp; both are in the index. The engine performs an index-only scan, never touching the main table

Without INCLUDE: the engine would need to fetch name from the main table for each qualifying row (a 'heap fetch'), which is slower on large tables.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the left-prefix rule with this example: an index on (country, city, postal_code). Which of the following queries can use this index? (a) WHERE country = 'UK', (b) WHERE city = 'London', (c) WHERE country = 'UK' AND city = 'London', (d) WHERE country = 'UK' AND postal_code = 'M1'.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) WHERE country = 'UK' — YES. Uses the leading column.
(b) WHERE city = 'London' — NO. The leading column (country) is not in the filter. The left-prefix rule is violated.
(c) WHERE country = 'UK' AND city = 'London' — YES. Uses the first two columns of the left prefix.
(d) WHERE country = 'UK' AND postal_code = 'M1' — PARTIAL. Can use the country column but not postal_code (city is missing in between). The engine uses the index to find country='UK' rows, then filters postal_code by scanning those rows.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the left-prefix rule for composite indexes, and describe what a covering index is and why it produces an index-only scan.

questions.prompt: An index on (A, B, C) can be used for which query?
questions.explanation: The left-prefix rule: a composite index on (A, B, C) is usable when the leftmost columns are present in the WHERE clause. (A, B) uses the first two prefix columns. Queries starting with B or C alone cannot use this index.

options: An index that contains all columns needed to satisfy a query — enabling an index-only scan without reading the main table
An index that covers all rows in the table
An index that covers both equality and range conditions
A partial index that covers only rows matching a WHERE condition
questions.answer: An index that contains all columns needed to satisfy a query — enabling an index-only scan without reading the main table
questions.explanation: A covering index stores all columns needed by the query (WHERE columns + SELECT columns). The engine can answer the query entirely from the index without fetching rows from the heap, which is much faster.

questions.prompt: For a query `WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`, which index is most effective?
questions.explanation: Start with the equality filter column (status) to narrow rows efficiently, then the ORDER BY column (created_at DESC) to avoid a separate sort. The engine can seek to status='active' rows, traverse them in created_at order, and stop at 20 rows.

questions.prompt: When would you choose a composite index over two separate single-column indexes?
options: When queries consistently filter on both columns together — the composite index is more efficient than combining two separate indexes
Composite indexes are always better than single-column indexes
When the columns are foreign keys
When one column is TEXT and the other is INTEGER
questions.answer: When queries consistently filter on both columns together — the composite index is more efficient than combining two separate indexes
questions.explanation: A composite index on (A, B) is a single, ordered structure that satisfies A+B filters in one seek. Two separate indexes on A and B require a 'bitmap AND' merge (expensive) or the engine uses just one index and filters the other in memory. When co-filters are predictable, composite is the right choice.
